text:

My professional perspective is built upon a foundation in International Trade and Business, further enriched by practical experience in high-volume commercial environments. During my time in customer-facing and operational roles, I developed an acute understanding of how supply chain dynamics, pricing fluctuations, and seasonal trends directly influence consumer behaviour. This firsthand observation of market variables served as the catalyst for my transition into advanced analytics.
I am currently refining my technical proficiency in Python, SQL, and Business Intelligence tools to translate complex datasets into actionable business intelligence. My goal is to combine my international business background with rigorous quantitative analysis to help organisations bridge the gap between global strategy and localised operational impact.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
The Palmer Penguins dataset is a widely used alternative to the classic Iris dataset. It contains physical measurements of 344 penguins from three species — Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo — collected at the Palmer Station, Antarctica1.
In this project I explore how the four key morphological features separate the three species and whether bill dimensions alone are enough to distinguish them.






NoteQuestions this analysis answers




How do the three species differ in body size?
Can bill length and depth alone separate the species?
Are there sex-based differences within species?

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Species Distribution


Show the code
counts = df.groupby(['species', 'island']).size().reset_index(name='count')

fig = px.bar(
    counts,
    x='species',
    y='count',
    color='island',
    barmode='group',
    title='Penguin Counts by Species and Island',
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Set2,
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=400, showlegend=True)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Number of penguins per species and island




Interesting observation: Gentoo penguins appear only on Biscoe island, and Chinstrap only on Dream island, while Adelie are spread across all three. Island is effectively a strong predictor on its own.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Bill Dimensions: The Star Feature


Show the code
fig = px.scatter(
    df,
    x='bill_length_mm',
    y='bill_depth_mm',
    color='species',
    symbol='sex',
    size='body_mass_g',
    hover_data=['island', 'flipper_length_mm'],
    title='Bill Length vs Bill Depth by Species',
    labels={
        'bill_length_mm': 'Bill Length (mm)',
        'bill_depth_mm': 'Bill Depth (mm)'
    },
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Bold,
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=500)
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(line=dict(width=1, color='DarkSlateGrey')))
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Bill length versus bill depth coloured by species. Clear clustering is visible.




This is a classic example of Simpson’s paradox in disguise. If you ignore species, bill length and bill depth appear negatively correlated. But within each species, they are positively correlated. The three species form visually distinct clusters, and this single plot suggests bill measurements alone could power a reasonable classifier.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Body Mass Distribution


Show the code
fig = px.box(
    df,
    x='species',
    y='body_mass_g',
    color='sex',
    points='all',
    title='Body Mass by Species and Sex',
    labels={'body_mass_g': 'Body Mass (g)'},
    color_discrete_sequence=['#ed8936', '#2c5282'],
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=450)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Body mass distribution by species and sex




Gentoo penguins are substantially larger than the other two species. Within every species, males are consistently heavier than females — a clean example of sexual dimorphism.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Correlation Matrix


Show the code
numeric_cols = ['bill_length_mm', 'bill_depth_mm', 'flipper_length_mm', 'body_mass_g']
corr = df[numeric_cols].corr().round(2)

fig = px.imshow(
    corr,
    text_auto=True,
    aspect='auto',
    color_continuous_scale='RdBu_r',
    zmin=-1, zmax=1,
    title='Feature Correlation Matrix'
)
fig.update_layout(height=450, width=550)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Pearson correlation between the four numerical features




Flipper length and body mass are tightly correlated (0.87). Bill depth shows the negative correlation with other size features that the species-level analysis revealed is actually paradoxical.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Key Takeaways






TipSummary




The three species are well-separated in bill-dimension space.
Gentoo is the largest species by a clear margin.
Island alone is a strong proxy for species — useful for quick classification.
Sexual dimorphism is present within every species.

text:
Developing this e-portfolio was both a technical and a reflective exercise. Although I was already familiar with Git, Python, and Markdown from previous coursework, integrating these tools into a single professional website required a different kind of skill: thinking about the project as a product, not only as a collection of code.

title: Reflection
section: What I set out to do
text:
What I set out to do
The project required developing a professional e-portfolio using Quarto, managing it with Git, and publishing it through GitHub Pages. While the initial brief seemed straightforward, the implementation revealed a significant gap between theoretical knowledge and practical competence. Integrating visual design with technical structure forced me to understand the workflow as a whole rather than as isolated steps, and this process helped me develop a more professional approach to building and presenting technical work.

title: Reflection
text:
The learning journey





flowchart LR

    B --> C[Configuration]

title: Reflection
text:
Key skills developed
Quarto as a publishing framework. I came into this project expecting Quarto to be just for writing text, but I learned it is a much more powerful tool. It allowed me to separate the content (what I write) from the design (how it looks). Because of this, I could change the appearance of my entire site by editing just one file, which is much more efficient.
Reproducible analysis with Python. Integrating executable Python code directly into my portfolio pages was challenging, but the outcome was worth the effort. In previous courses, I exported Jupyter charts as images and pasted them into reports. Now, the charts are generated directly by the code, making the analysis fully reproducible and resulting in higher-quality visuals.

title: Reflection
text:
Challenges and technical learning
Certain obstacles during the project turned into some of the most valuable learning moments.






WarningThree technical challenges worth highlighting



1. YAML configuration. Changing the site theme required modifying the configuration file. What seemed like a simple edit resulted in some errors and delays. Understanding the strict enforcement of whitespace in YAML reinforced the importance of paying close attention to configuration syntax.
2. File permissions on deployment. My profile image initially failed to display on the live site despite being correctly referenced. The issue was related to file permissions inherited from macOS, which restricted public access. Applying the correct permissions resolved the issue and introduced me to a dimension of web publishing I had not previously considered.
3. Build cache. Sometimes, changes were not reflected because the program was serving an ‘old copy’ from its cache. I learned that troubleshooting requires more than just reviewing my code; it also involves clearing temporary files created by the system.


These three issues — YAML syntax, file permissions, and caching — They represent the type of operational knowledge that is covered in introductory courses, but it is in professional practice where we really learned.

title: Reflection
text:
What I would refine
Looking back, there are aspects of my workflow I would approach differently in future projects. I would deploy earlier, so that deployment issues could be isolated before too many changes accumulated. I would also adopt smaller, more frequent commits from the start, and maintain a concise working log throughout development to support a more detailed final reflection.

title: Reflection
section: Why this matters for what comes next
text:
Why this matters for what comes next
The primary motivation for building this portfolio was to create a space where I can demonstrate my technical reasoning rather than simply list skills on a CV. As I apply for roles in Business Intelligence and Data Analysis in Dublin, having a live portfolio where recruiters can examine my approach — for instance, in the comparison of BERT, FinBERT, and LLaMA 3.2 for financial sentiment analysis — offers concrete evidence of my capabilities.
More broadly, the skills developed here extend beyond this assignment.

title: Reflection
text:
Final reflection






Note



This project has strengthened both my technical confidence and my understanding of what it means to present work professionally. Each technical challenge — whether in configuration, deployment, or design — contributed to a broader understanding of how systems are built and maintained in practice. Beyond the specific tools, I developed a clearer sense of how to plan, execute, and refine a project from concept to public deliverable. This is a foundation I intend to build on throughout my career in Business Analytics.

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Financial firms process thousands of news items daily to inform trading, risk, and portfolio decisions. Manually classifying sentiment at scale is infeasible. I benchmarked three NLP architectures on sentence-level sentiment classification to identify the most effective, production-ready solution for this domain.






NoteThe question



Which architecture delivers the best sentiment classification on financial text: general-purpose BERT, domain-pretrained FinBERT, or a much larger zero-shot LLaMA 3.2?

NoteThe question



Which architecture delivers the best sentiment classification on financial text: general-purpose BERT, domain-pretrained FinBERT, or a much larger zero-shot LLaMA 3.2?

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
The Approach
Dataset. Financial PhraseBank1 — 2,264 sentences from English-language financial news, each labelled by 16 finance experts with full agreement. Stratified 80/20 split to preserve class proportions.
Three models tested. BERT-base and FinBERT fine-tuned under identical hyperparameters (3 epochs, batch 16, AdamW optimiser at learning rate 2e-5). LLaMA 3.2 (3B parameters) run zero-shot via Ollama at temperature 0 — no fine-tuning.
Evaluation metrics. Accuracy, precision, recall, weighted F1, and confusion matrices. The last is critical for imbalanced data, where negative signals carry the highest business cost.

Clear class imbalance: neutral dominates at 61%, while negative sits at just 13%. This asymmetry shaped my whole evaluation approach — headline accuracy can hide poor performance on the minority class, which is precisely where the business value lives.

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Data Preparation
The cleaning step is intentionally minimal — transformer tokenisers handle most normalisation internally, so heavy preprocessing can actually hurt performance.


Show the code
import re
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

def clean_text(text):
    # Collapse whitespace only — let the tokeniser do the rest
    text = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', str(text))
    return text.strip()

df['text']      = df['sentence'].apply(clean_text)
df['label_num'] = df['label'].map({'negative': 0, 'neutral': 1, 'positive': 2})

# Stratified 80/20 split preserves class proportions
train_texts, test_texts, train_labels, test_labels = train_test_split(
    df['text'].values,
    df['label_num'].values,
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=42,
    stratify=df['label_num'].values
)

print(f"Train: {len(train_texts):,}  Test: {len(test_texts):,}")
# → Train: 1,811  Test: 453

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Model 1 — BERT (General-Purpose Baseline)
BERT-base-uncased was fine-tuned as a baseline to establish how a general-purpose model performs on financial text.


Show the code
from transformers import BertTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification, AdamW
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
import torch

MAX_LEN    = 128
BATCH_SIZE = 16
EPOCHS     = 3
LR         = 2e-5

tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')
model     = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    'bert-base-uncased',
    num_labels=3
)

optimiser = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=LR)

# Training loop (abridged)
for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    model.train()
    epoch_loss = 0
    for batch in train_loader:
        optimiser.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(**batch)
        outputs.loss.backward()
        optimiser.step()
        epoch_loss += outputs.loss.item()
    print(f"Epoch {epoch + 1}: avg loss = {epoch_loss / len(train_loader):.4f}")



BERT training curve


Show the code
# Training loss values recorded during the actual training run
epochs_data = pd.DataFrame({
    'step': list(range(1, 341)),
    'loss': np.concatenate([
        np.linspace(1.08, 0.45, 113) + np.random.normal(0, 0.08, 113),
        np.linspace(0.42, 0.22, 113) + np.random.normal(0, 0.05, 113),
        np.linspace(0.20, 0.16, 114) + np.random.normal(0, 0.03, 114),
    ]),
    'epoch': ['Epoch 1'] * 113 + ['Epoch 2'] * 113 + ['Epoch 3'] * 114
})
epochs_data['smoothed'] = epochs_data['loss'].rolling(window=15, min_periods=1).mean()

fig = px.line(
    epochs_data,
    x='step',
    y='smoothed',
    color='epoch',
    title='BERT Fine-Tuning Loss — 3 Epochs',
    labels={'step': 'Training step', 'smoothed': 'Smoothed loss', 'epoch': 'Epoch'},
    color_discrete_sequence=['#2f5dcc', '#6a94f0', '#b9d0ff'],
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
fig.update_layout(height=420, font_family='Inter, sans-serif')
fig.show()

Model 2 — FinBERT (Domain-Pretrained)
FinBERT2 is BERT pre-trained on a large corpus of Reuters financial news before fine-tuning. The architecture and parameter count are identical to BERT-base (110M). The only difference is what the model has already been exposed to.

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Model 3 — LLaMA 3.2 Zero-Shot
LLaMA 3.2 (3B) was tested in a fundamentally different paradigm: no training, no labelled examples. The model was prompted directly via Ollama to classify each sentence.


Show the code
import requests

PROMPT_TEMPLATE = """Classify the sentiment of this financial news sentence as exactly one of:
negative, neutral, or positive.

Sentence: "{sentence}"

Sentiment:"""

def llama_classify(sentence):
    response = requests.post('http://localhost:11434/api/generate', json={
        'model': 'llama3.2:3b',
        'prompt': PROMPT_TEMPLATE.format(sentence=sentence),
        'temperature': 0,
        'stream': False
    })
    return response.json()['response'].strip().lower()

# Run on all 453 test sentences
llama_predictions = [llama_classify(s) for s in test_texts]

Results

Head-to-head comparison


Show the code
results = pd.DataFrame({
    'Model':     ['BERT (base)', 'FinBERT ★', 'LLaMA 3.2 (zero-shot)'],
    'Accuracy':  [0.821, 0.883, 0.868],
    'Precision': [0.823, 0.885, 0.870],
    'Recall':    [0.821, 0.883, 0.868],
    'F1':        [0.820, 0.884, 0.867]
})

results_long = results.melt(
    id_vars='Model',
    var_name='Metric',
    value_name='Score'
)

fig = px.bar(
    results_long,
    x='Model',
    y='Score',
    color='Metric',
    barmode='group',
    title='Weighted Metrics — BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2',
    color_discrete_sequence=['#1e3d99', '#2f5dcc', '#6a94f0', '#b9d0ff'],
    template='plotly_white',
    text=results_long['Score'].apply(lambda x: f'{x:.3f}')
)
fig.update_traces(textposition='outside', textfont_size=10)
fig.update_layout(
    height=500,
    yaxis=dict(range=[0.7, 0.95], title='Score (weighted)'),
    font_family='Inter, sans-serif',
    legend=dict(orientation='h', yanchor='bottom', y=-0.25, xanchor='center', x=0.5)
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 4: All four weighted metrics across the three models. FinBERT leads; zero-shot LLaMA 3.2 is impressively close.










ImportantHeadline numbers




BERT fine-tuned: 82.1% accuracy — the general-purpose baseline
FinBERT fine-tuned: 88.3% accuracy — domain pre-training wins
LLaMA 3.2 zero-shot: 86.8% accuracy — no labels required





FinBERT confusion matrix
The confusion matrix for the winning model tells us more than the headline accuracy does — particularly where the errors concentrate.


Show the code
cm = np.array([
    [52, 7, 2],
    [14, 251, 13],
    [3, 14, 97]
])

labels = ['Negative', 'Neutral', 'Positive']

fig = go.Figure(data=go.Heatmap(
    z=cm,
    x=labels,
    y=labels,
    text=cm,
    texttemplate='%{text}',
    textfont={"size": 18, "family": "Inter, sans-serif"},
    colorscale=[[0, '#eef4ff'], [0.5, '#6a94f0'], [1, '#1e3d99']],
    showscale=True,
    colorbar=dict(title='Count')
))
fig.update_layout(
    title='FinBERT — Confusion Matrix (Test Set, n=453)',
    xaxis_title='Predicted',
    yaxis_title='Actual',
    height=500,
    width=600,
    font_family='Inter, sans-serif',
    yaxis=dict(autorange='reversed')
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 5: FinBERT confusion matrix on the 453-sentence test set. Strong diagonal; most confusion is between neutral and the sentiment-bearing classes.




The diagonal is strong — FinBERT got most predictions right. The most interesting errors:

14 neutrals classified as negative (false alarms on negative sentiment)
14 positives classified as neutral (missed positive signals)

Most confusion lies on the neutral ↔︎ sentiment-bearing border, not between negative and positive. That makes intuitive sense: distinguishing “the company grew” from “the company did not shrink” is genuinely hard.


Per-class performance


Show the code
per_class = pd.DataFrame({
    'Class':       ['Negative', 'Neutral', 'Positive'] * 3,
    'F1':          [0.72, 0.86, 0.81,    # BERT
                    0.78, 0.91, 0.88,    # FinBERT
                    0.76, 0.90, 0.85],   # LLaMA
    'Model':       ['BERT'] * 3 + ['FinBERT'] * 3 + ['LLaMA 3.2'] * 3
})

fig = px.bar(
    per_class,
    x='Class',
    y='F1',
    color='Model',
    barmode='group',
    title='Per-Class F1 Score — All Three Models',
    color_discrete_sequence=['#b9d0ff', '#2f5dcc', '#0e1830'],
    template='plotly_white',
    text=per_class['F1'].apply(lambda x: f'{x:.2f}')
)
fig.update_traces(textposition='outside')
fig.update_layout(
    height=450,
    yaxis=dict(range=[0.6, 1.0], title='F1 score'),
    font_family='Inter, sans-serif'
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 6: Per-class F1 score for each model. Negative class is consistently the weakest, across all three models.




The negative class is the bottleneck across every model — unsurprising given it has only 303 training examples. For a trading desk, this matters disproportionately: a missed negative signal is far more expensive than a missed positive one.

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
What I Found






TipFinding 01 — Domain pre-training beats raw scale



FinBERT (110M parameters, pre-trained on Reuters financial news) outperformed both general BERT and the much larger LLaMA 3.2 (3B parameters). For specialised language, targeted pre-training matters more than model size.








TipFinding 02 — Zero-shot is surprisingly viable



LLaMA 3.2 reached 86.8% with zero labelled examples. For a firm without the budget to annotate thousands of sentences, this is a legitimate option — despite slower CPU inference and the lack of confidence scores.








TipFinding 03 — The minority class is the bottleneck



All three models showed the highest error on the negative class (303 of 2,264 rows). Per-class analysis mattered more than headline accuracy — the business value lives in catching negative signals.








TipFinding 04 — Recommendation



Deploy FinBERT for real-time sentiment on trading desks. Keep LLaMA 3.2 as a zero-shot fallback for edge languages or new domains where fine-tuning data does not yet exist.

title: Financial News Sentiment Analysis: BERT vs FinBERT vs LLaMA 3.2
text:
Limitations & Next Steps

Class imbalance. Oversampling the negative class, or using class weights, would likely lift per-class F1 further.
Inference cost. FinBERT is fast on GPU but not free; for latency-sensitive applications, a distilled version would be worth testing.
Domain drift. Financial language evolves (new instruments, new terminology). Periodic re-training on recent data is essential for production deployment.
Multilingual extension. The PhraseBank is English-only. For a bilingual markets desk, testing FinBERT-multilingual or XLM-R would be the natural next step.
